sections.title: Character and personal qualities
sections.lead: How you are built and what people see in you at first glance.

positions.label: Personality portrait
positions.text: Arcanum “The Hanged Man” · A · The first impression is built around one theme: a pause and a different angle — the one who agreed to wait comes out ahead. At their strongest they can wait without panic; under strain they play the victim and keep a tally. The image turns into a steady reputation once they can tell a meaningful pause from the habit of enduring.

positions.label: Spiritual task
positions.text: Arcanum “Justice” · B · A spiritual task you are born with switches on by itself: balance and honesty — weighs things up and calls them by their names. So the person may not count it as a gift that the person sees the tilt and names it plainly; the other side shows when the person passes sentence on people instead of understanding them. The mature task of this position is to ask the other side before you draw a conclusion.

positions.label: Material task
positions.text: Arcanum “The World” · C · The material task moves the theme of wholeness and scale — one room and one role feel too small — from intention to result. The strong side shows in deeds: they think in long stretches and see them through; when it tips over, they talk about grand things and forget the people close by. This position is lived not by a promise but by a readiness to build a whole out of what is already there instead of waiting for the full set.

interactions.title: Outer image and inner task
paragraphs: How the first impression relates to what drives the person from within. In this order The Hanged Man takes position A — personality portrait: The first impression is built around one theme: a pause and a different angle — the one who agreed to wait comes out ahead. Justice takes position B — spiritual task: A spiritual task you are born with switches on by itself: balance and honesty — weighs things up and calls them by their names. So the person may not count it as a gift that the person sees the tilt and names it plainly; the other side shows when the person passes sentence on people instead of understanding them.

At its strongest, at position A a person can wait without panic, and at position B — a person sees an imbalance and names it directly. The pair works in tune when the first quality sets its own stage and the second does not argue with it but continues it in its own role.

Tension appears when at position A a person plays the victim and keeps score, and at position B — a person judges people instead of understanding them. This link is best checked as a sequence: what was shown or intended first, and which action the situation ended with.

Justice demands clarity, The Hanged Man refuses to let anyone hurry, so this person decides slowly and almost never gets it wrong. In arguments they win by time: while the others heat up, they gather facts.

Waiting for the truth stretches into years: the person expects fairness to restore itself. Usually it does not. One direct step, such as a written claim, a conversation or a court case, is worth ten years of patient resentment.

longform.summary: The triple 12–8–21 joins three different tasks: The Hanged Man sets the first impression, Justice works from the inside, and The World tests the character through actions. Wholeness here comes not from identical qualities but from the ability to translate one into another.
longform.strength: The main strength of the triple shows when a person at once can wait without panic, sees an imbalance and names it directly and, in practical decisions, thinks in long periods and carries them through. Then the outer image does not diverge from the inner motive, and what was promised is confirmed by an action.
longform.tension: On the outer level the risk looks like this: a person plays the victim and keeps score. From the inside the tension shows when a person judges people instead of understanding them. In material decisions the tension settles in when a person reasons about great things and forgets those close by. These are not three verdicts but three places where one and the same episode of life can be checked against the facts.
longform.practice: Take one situation that repeats in the coming week and answer three questions in writing: what impression do I make, what do I actually want, and which action will confirm it. It is better to start from the strong side of position C: a person thinks in long periods and carries them through. After you act, compare the result with the original image — that turns the triple into a working observation rather than a set of labels.

sections.title: Your purpose
sections.lead: Four levels: personal, social, spiritual and planetary.

positions.label: Personal purpose
positions.text: Arcanum “The Sun” · personal · With no audience the person would choose this theme: clarity and warmth, around them everything is clearer and easier, themselves included. Staying true to themselves is visible in that they make hard things clear and light; walking away from their task shows in that they depend on attention and go dim without it. This position comes alive when they manage to check whether they are shining or waiting for someone to shine on them.

positions.label: Social purpose
positions.text: Arcanum “Judgement” · social · Others can lean on this theme: a summing-up and a calling — they gather what has been done and call others to do their own. In shared work they are most useful when they hear their calling and follow it; the role stops working when they live under someone else’s assessment. A concrete choice creates steady use instead of an image: answer the call with an action this year, not “someday”.

positions.label: Spiritual purpose
positions.text: Arcanum “The Hanged Man” · spiritual · The personal and social levels are joined by the theme “a pause and a different angle — the one who agreed to wait comes out ahead”. Agreement with themselves is felt when they can wait without panic; the inner argument comes back when they play the victim and keep a tally. Tying the two levels into one direction takes a readiness to tell a meaningful pause from the habit of enduring.

positions.label: Planetary purpose
positions.text: Arcanum “The Hierophant” · planetary · The theme of leaning on knowledge and tradition — explaining so that things become clear — reaches beyond a personal biography. The contribution becomes visible to many when the person explains complicated things briefly and to the point; the scale stays a pretty idea if they give lectures where help was asked for. Starting from real influence rather than a loud role comes from one decision: leave the other person room to disagree.

tripleReading.title: Material karma
tripleReading.topic: Task, attitude and the entry to money
tripleReading.heading: Big plans need room for other people
paragraphs: The bigger the plan, the clearer it becomes that people work differently. Here the World sets your material task: allowing that variety into a shared undertaking, rather than treating your own route as the only sensible one. The Chariot shapes thoughts about earning and possessions around progress towards a goal: stopping can easily feel like defeat. The Emperor at the entry of the money line calls for structure, with clear responsibilities. Taken too far, this becomes a wish to control every step and every decision others make.

Say you are organising a house move. There are things to pack, a van to arrange and a new home to prepare. Someone packs boxes differently from you, and you want to redo them, although their method works. **A big undertaking needs a shared outcome and people free to do their part.** You can agree that the crockery must arrive intact while leaving the packing method to your helper. In earning, the Emperor brings this into taking responsibility for a specific result; trying to manage every detail yourself can hold up work before the arrangements are even agreed.

The difficulty can grow from wanting to get life settled quickly and protect it from other people’s mistakes. Expanding the undertaking may then mean only that you have more people to supervise. Every disagreement looks like an obstacle, and each new possibility becomes another reason to give orders. Time, willing help and the freedom you wanted in the first place can all be lost. Ask yourself: “What result do I need, and which ways of achieving it am I leaving to others?” In your next shared task, hand over one small job in full, agreeing only the outcome and deadline.

positions.label: Outer expression

At their strongest they can wait without panic; under strain they play the victim and keep a tally. positions.text: Helping a younger person learn and move towards a goal may be exciting for you. The Chariot connects your role as the adult with direction, effort, and visible progress. The difficulty is turning the experience into a race. You might suggest another competition before asking whether the activity still interests them. Your ability to organise can be more helpful when it also allows for their pace. Whose goal are you working towards, and how much say does the child have in choosing it?

positions.text: Arcanum “The Fool” · J · The outer portrait A joins the centre E through the theme ‘freedom and lightness — starting from a clean sheet as many times as it takes’. If the passage is free, the person begins again without fear and without baggage; if the role argues with the inner state, they run away from responsibility. Bringing outside and inside into line takes one decision: to choose commitments deliberately instead of putting every one of them off.

tripleReading.title: Parent-child line
tripleReading.topic: Childhood, attitude to children and outer expression
tripleReading.heading: Keep your own life moving while helping theirs
paragraphs: An open, loosely structured family life can leave you with a strong wish to give the next generation a clear route. The Fool in the parents position represents moving freely towards experience, without a path laid out in advance. The Chariot in your attitude to children may respond in the opposite way: setting a goal, focusing effort and helping someone reach a result. Meanwhile, The Hanged Man in your outer expression pauses your own progress. To keep someone else moving, you may repeatedly revise your plans, see the situation from their position and put your original decision on hold. The question is whether that pause still serves a purpose.

For example, you promise to help a teenager you know prepare an application for an educational project. The task is clear and the deadline close, so you set out the steps. They send the next section later than agreed, and you rearrange your evening to finish in time anyway. **Help loses its balance when someone else's goal keeps moving at the cost of your life standing still.** There is a useful ability here to understand a difficulty and find another way. But the route stops being shared if only your plans can change, while their deadline and workload remain fixed.

In trying to avoid repeating uncertainty, you may hold on too tightly to someone else's result. Each delay then requires another sacrifice of your own plans. A change of perspective no longer opens up options; it only explains why you must give way again. You remain in charge of progress while standing still yourself. Ask yourself: 'Which part of this goal needs my involvement, and which am I still carrying out of habit?' For your next offer of help, define one complete piece of work, after which you return to your own plan.

sections.title: Karmic tail
sections.lead: The karmic tail: what came here together with you.

positions.label: Entry of the relationship line and the tail
positions.text: Arcanum “The Devil” · M · At the fork between relationships and the karmic tail this comes out: passion and matter: it gives a powerful pull and the bill that comes with it. The first reaction helps closeness when the person knows how to want and to get material things, and it starts the old script when they fall into dependence — on people, on things, on work. What keeps them off the circle is a pause in which they can check who makes the decisions in the pair of “me and my desire”.

positions.label: Middle point of the tail
positions.text: Summing up someone else’s life is the reaction that comes ready-made. The ability to see the whole is already trained: this person quickly sees where things are going and is not fooled by details. Close people are judged by past actions, the sentence is passed in silence and never reviewed. Take one old grievance and either say it out loud or close it for good.

positions.label: Karmic task
positions.text: Arcanum “The Hierophant” · D · This is not a punishment but a story that keeps returning: leaning on knowledge and tradition, explaining things so that they become clear. The grown-up answer begins where the person explains complicated things briefly and to the point, and the old circle begins with the opposite: they give lectures where help was asked for. One concrete decision breaks the repeat — leave the other person room to disagree.

paragraphs: “I’ll let my ears freeze off to spite Mum”: this Russian saying fits the 15-20-5 tail better than the legend behind its name, the “Rebel”. The legend says that in a past life the soul, born into a family with strict rules, rebelled: chose passion over duty, then left or was cast out. None of this can be checked. As metaphor, though, the legend is precise, and the cards themselves back it.

For Waite, the Devil is “the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden when those are driven forth therefrom who have eaten the forbidden fruit”. Breaking a commandment and landing outside the gates: that is the Rebel’s plot. His raised right hand, Waite says, is “the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant in the fifth card” — and the Hierophant is this tail’s root. The Waite–Smith cards share one layout: a raised figure with a lifted hand above two figures, kneeling ministers on the Hierophant, a chained pair on the Devil.

The gesture is not an absence of blessing but its reverse: the same raised hand, turned the other way. A protest mirrors the rule it fights. Hence the saying: whoever acts out of spite still lets Mum decide what they do, only with the sign reversed. The Rebel of 15-20-5 is not a person without rules. **It is a person whose life is built around someone else’s rule with a minus sign.**

paragraphs.h3: Chained not to the fruit but to the ban

paragraphs: Here the Devil’s pull is lit by a ban. A cigarette behind the garages at fourteen. A partner the family will never accept: the union rests on “us against the world”, and once the parents come round, the passion somehow fades. Forbidden fruit has become just fruit.

Waite’s card shows why. The chain loops round the neck, the hands are free, and it runs not to the fruit, not to each other, but to a ring on the altar of the figure towering above. Our reading: **a person with this tail is tied not to the forbidden thing but to the ban.** Without the ban, many desires quietly vanish.

paragraphs.h3: No judge on the Judgement card

paragraphs: On Waite’s twentieth card an angel sounds the trumpet and the dead rise — not punishment but transformation “in answer to the summons of the Supernal — which summons is heard and answered from within”. Waite asks: “What is that within us which does sound a trumpet and all that is lower in our nature rises in response — almost in a moment, almost in the twinkling of an eye?” That lower nature is exactly what the Devil card depicts.

In 15-20-5 the trumpet sounds from outside: “time to grow up” from Mum, “that’s not how we do things here” from the boss. Everything lower rises in the twinkling of an eye — hurt, stubbornness, the urge to prove a point — and a sharp turn follows: slam the door, quit, start from zero. It feels like resurrection, but another voice set the new life’s direction.

The card’s Russian name, Sud, also means “court of law” — and hints at another trap: judgement as a tribunal. For years an argument runs in the head with a father, a teacher, an ex, all long out of the picture. Yet Waite’s card has no scales and no sword; those belong to Justice, the eighth card. The angel hands down no verdict; he calls, and the judgement, Wen stresses, is the person’s own. **The circle runs on a double substitution: a verdict replaces the call, and someone else’s judgement replaces one’s own.**

The centre of the chart holds the circle tightest: everyone with this tail has 10 there, the Wheel of Fortune, the comfort zone. A break feels less like a problem than “a new chapter”. But for Waite the wheel’s essential idea is “stability amidst movement”, and a wheel without an axle can only spin. Each new order hardens into a new altar with a new ring: yesterday’s rebel starts a business “so that nobody tells me what to do”, and within a few years its rules are stricter than the old boss’s.

paragraphs.h3: Two sons chained to the same altar

paragraphs: The parable of the prodigal son reads like this circle. The parallel is ours, not Waite’s or the method’s. The younger son “wasted his substance with riotous living” — the Devil. “When he came to himself”, he went home, and his father would say he “was dead, and is alive again” — Judgement. The father has a ring put on his hand — the Hierophant and his blessing.

The elder son never left. Hearing of the feast, he “was angry, and would not go in”: “Lo, these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment.” He carried the chain as a duty. His father answers: “Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine.” These are the two faces of 15-20-5: the open rebel who argues and leaves, and the quiet one who does everything properly and nurses grievances for years. **Both are chained to the same altar: one through “against”, the other through “must”.** The parable never says whether the elder son went in. Nobody else can take that step.

paragraphs.h3: The way out is written into the Devil’s own description

paragraphs: The figure towering over the chained pair, Waite writes, is himself a bondsman, “blind to the liberty of service”. The ministers on Waite’s fifth card kneel without chains. The Hierophant’s divinatory list opens with “marriage, alliance” and goes on to “captivity, servitude”. One bond can be a vow or a captivity; the only difference is whether it was chosen.
The root’s task is neither a return to obedience nor a hunt for the “right church”, but taking the Hierophant’s place oneself: choosing what to serve and being able to explain one’s rules.

Sort one’s rules into “for” and “against”. In “I will never be like my father”, the father is still in charge.
Find one thing to keep from the family line, faith or former surroundings, and say so out loud to the person it came from.

paragraphs: If there was violence or danger in the family, safety matters more than any scheme, this one included.

paragraphs.h3: The one who left and became a place to come back to

paragraphs: In the worked-through version, the Devil gives the courage to go where it is “not allowed” and an inside knowledge of the forbidden. Judgement gives the skill to change a life once it has truly run its course, not merely when hurt. The Hierophant gives a form that can be passed on: rules with reasons. Such people get called in when the old order has broken down and no new one exists yet. They will not hold anyone on the chain of “that’s how it’s done”: they know its weight.

Of the figure towering over the chained pair, Waite writes that he is “not to be their master for ever”. The Hierophant of this tail is not someone who never left. **It is someone who left, understood why they left, and became a place others can come back to.**

sections.title: Chakras: the energy map, reading the seven levels
sections.lead: Seven levels in three columns: matter, energy and feelings.

longform.title: Chakras: the energy map, reading the seven levels for matrix 12–8–21
longform.lead: It begins with what gives you a sense of home. Then come desire, action, relationships, words and understanding. Last comes meaning — the reason you want to keep going. This is a symbolic portrait drawn from your matrix: seven chakras, each showing a different side of one life.

chakraRows.title: Muladhara
chakraRows.heading: Where custom keeps everything even
paragraphs: Your daily life strives to be complete: the World in Muladhara is a home where everything has found its place and come together as one whole. The Hierophant helps you keep that fullness by leaning on what is established: family traditions, tried and tested rules, “this is how we do things”. When something is disrupted, you return to what has stood the test of time. And you feel settled inside when Justice is at work: everyone’s portion is measured fairly, and no one carries more than the rest.

Take a family cottage shared for many years. Everyone has their own vegetable beds and their own weekends, the costs of the fence and the water are split by an old rule, and in August everyone gathers to make jam — because it has always been so. No one argues over who owes what: the order answers for itself. **Your footing is a way of life where everything has long been in its place and everyone has their fair share.** In a home like that you can relax: the rules are known, and nobody will be left out.

It becomes vulnerable when someone new enters this finished world. A new member of the family with habits of their own — and a suggestion to change something sounds like a threat to the balance. “That’s how we do things here” becomes the main argument, and the newcomer’s request is weighed on the old scales, which have no room for it. It is hard for a newcomer to belong where everything has already been allotted, and hard for you to notice that the wholeness rests on closed doors.

chakraRows.title: Svadhisthana
chakraRows.heading: Steering desire, rejoicing openly
paragraphs: The strength of your desire shows at once. The Devil feeds a pull towards whatever feels good — tasty food, the thrill of the game, bodily pleasures, anything that takes hold of you completely and will not wait. The Emperor governs how this plays out in life: you set the limits yourself, choose where, when and how much, and keep the promises you make to yourself. And the Sun colours what remains afterwards — a simple, bright joy without a shadow, like that of a child with nothing to apologise for.

**In your hands, strong desire becomes a celebration, not a disaster.** You can treat yourself to a real feast, a long game, a trip just for one favourite cuisine — and carry it off so that there is nothing to regret in the morning. Order does not put out passion; it gives it shape. That is why your pleasure comes out bright: you want to share it, it is easy to talk about, and there is nothing in it that needs hiding.

The danger is that the limits slowly come to matter more than the pleasure itself. It feels good to have power over your own cravings, and the rules multiply: how much is allowed, when it has been earned, what counts as excess. The desire does not go anywhere; it simply answers now to the routine rather than to you. Every unplanned joy feels like a defeat, and sunny simplicity gives way to the dry satisfaction of having held back once again.

chakraRows.title: Manipura
chakraRows.heading: Hearing that it is time for the next turn
paragraphs: You act best when you sense movement. In your work the Wheel of Fortune gives you a knack for handling its turns: noticing that circumstances have shifted, rearranging the plan and making use of the right moment. As motivation, the same Wheel brings the thrill of change — your energy rises when things get moving and a new opportunity opens up. Outcomes are felt through Judgement. Success or failure sounds to you like the angel’s trumpet on the card: the moment it becomes clear that this stage is over and it is time to rise to the next.

**Any turn can become a beginning for you if you hear what it means.** A project falls through — and you see what it taught you and where to go next. Luck comes your way — and you do not just celebrate; you understand what new role it opens up. Here will does not fight the course of events but answers it in good time.

You are most vulnerable in a lull. When the wheel barely turns, the work seems to have lost its point, and you want to wait for a new sign: an offer, a change, that very call. You try every small event on for size: is this it? Meanwhile the work, which needs ordinary, regular steps, stands still. Acting on your own initiative quietly turns into waiting for a signal, and circumstances start deciding for you.

chakraRows.title: Anahata
chakraRows.heading: Holding together through the turns
paragraphs: For you, love proves itself through what repeats: the call you agreed on, the shared dinner, the promise no one needs reminding of. This is how the Hierophant shows up in closeness — through settled routine and keeping your word. What holds you in a relationship is the Wheel of Fortune: an interest in where it is going, in new stages and turns that cannot be mapped out in advance. The Devil makes your experience of connection strong and tenacious: when you attach, you do so in earnest, and the very thought of loss cuts deep.

**Your bond can survive change because it has something to stand on.** Say your job changes, or your city, or the familiar rhythm of your days. The Wheel keeps the relationship from standing still, while your customs remind you that you are still together. A ritual may change its form — dinner becomes an evening phone call — but its meaning stays. Strong feeling works in the bond’s favour: you care, and you look for ways to stay close in new circumstances.

As long as the turn is shared, it inspires you. But if only your loved one changes — perhaps they have taken up something new or started keeping evenings of their own — attachment whispers that this is how you lose someone. Then a custom turns into a test: “we always used to…”, “if you love me, stay the way you were”. The rule that protected the bond starts holding the person in place. They may stay by your side out of duty rather than desire — and that is exactly what strong attachment fears most.

chakraRows.title: Vishuddha
chakraRows.heading: Asking outright what hangs in the air
paragraphs: A change in someone’s tone is hard for you to let pass unnoticed. The Moon in your Vishuddha explains what draws you into such conversations: a sensitivity to tone, to pauses, to what sounds between the words. And you speak like the Fool — simply and directly, without meaningful hints: “Is it just me, or did something upset you?” Calm comes with the Emperor, when what was unclear gets a clear answer and it’s obvious how to go on.

Say a colleague on a shared project suddenly starts giving one-word replies and stops joking in the chat. You message them privately: “Listen, I get the feeling something about the plan is bothering you. Just tell me straight.” It turns out they were landed with someone else’s task and felt awkward objecting. Half an hour later the tasks have been reshuffled. **After your question, a vague tension can become a clear agreement.** And you feel at ease: everything has been said, and it’s clear who is doing what.

Asked too often, “Are you OK?” can lose its weight. You hear every pause distinctly, and asking costs nothing: “Are you sure everything’s fine? You’re not upset?” Your calm returns only after a clear “Yes, really”, and so the questions keep coming. Someone close to you answers in detail at first, then on autopilot. And one day something real is hiding behind the usual “I’m fine”, and by now it’s hard to pick out: the stock reply has become the easiest way to end the conversation.

cells.title: Emotions
cells.caption: The calm of a clear answer

chakraRows.title: Ajna
chakraRows.heading: Getting to the truth without getting stuck
paragraphs: For you, an unclear situation is like an open case. The Chariot sets your way of thinking: an inquiry is a journey to a destination, step by step, past every obstacle. Justice is the fuel — the wish to find out what really happened, to separate facts from rumours and to give each party what their actions deserve. And the feeling belongs to the Devil: an unanswered question hooks you hard, and until there is an answer, your mind keeps going back to it.

A company has charged you twice and keeps replying with stock phrases. Someone else would shrug it off, but you gather receipts, emails and the contract, find the right clause and write a letter that can’t be answered with a template. **You carry an inquiry through to a fair outcome long after everyone else has grown tired.** A week later the money is back, and you are left with a neat folder and the satisfaction of someone who refused to be confused.

Yet not every case deserves a grip that tight. Unresolved unfairness holds you like a chain: in the evening you reread the emails in your head, hunt for better wording, imagine what the other side will say. The cost of the inquiry keeps rising, but stopping is hard — backing down feels like losing rather than choosing. At some point you are no longer driving the Chariot; it is driving you. The truth has long been clear, yet the question still won’t let go.

chakraRows.title: Sahasrara
chakraRows.heading: A pause that changes course
paragraphs: Sometimes meaning becomes clear not on the run but when you stop. In your actions this is the Hanged Man: you can step out of the usual flow of things and look at your life from an unfamiliar angle. That look is not idle — Justice guides it, a set of inner scales on which you honestly weigh what you put in and what you get back. And the outcome feels like Judgement: a call you cannot leave unanswered, a clear “it’s time”, after which your old life no longer seems the only one possible.

Picture a quiet week between two projects. You don’t rush; you calmly sort through what your current work gives you, what it costs and what you are really serving. The sums don’t add up — and that brings relief rather than bitterness. **Your turning points come not from resentment or exhaustion but from an honest look from the outside.** That is why a decision made after such a pause holds firm: you know exactly why you are doing what you do.

It gets harder when the review turns into a trial of the past. The scales keep working: how many years went the wrong way, where you should have made up your mind sooner, who is to blame. The pause drags on, and instead of a new step there is an inquiry. The call that started it all grows fainter while you weigh not the choice any more but yourself. The past was the road to your present clarity, but in this kind of reckoning it looks like one long debt.

energyField.title: Overall energy field
energyField.topic: The shared tone of all seven levels
energyField.heading: A quiet strength with no witnesses
paragraphs: Most of your work happens with no audience. In what you do, you are like the Hermit: you take on a task yourself, go at your own pace and don’t call for help until you have worked it out. Your energy comes from Strength — inner steadiness, the ability to come to terms gently with your own fear and steer it where it won’t get in the way. And your feelings are kept by the High Priestess: you understand and feel many things deeply, but keep them to yourself, behind the veil.

**Your strength works quietly: calm on the outside, and inside a great deal of work that no one sees.** Suppose a hard stretch arrives: a difficult exam, uncertainty at work, a move to another city. You don’t complain or panic. Each evening you simply sit down, work out the next step and persuade your anxiety to wait. People around you are amazed at how easily it all came to you. They didn’t see the nights when you were holding your lion.

That is exactly the difficulty: since no one sees, no one offers help. The High Priestess keeps her knowledge to herself, the Hermit walks alone, and Strength won’t let you show how frightening it sometimes is. Those close to you get used to the idea that you will cope, and stop asking. So when one day your strength runs short, it will not be easy to say so: for too long you have looked like someone who needs no support. A solitude that began as your own way of doing things becomes a habit for everyone around you.

sections.title: Reading by decades up to 80
sections.lead: Which energy leads you through each decade.

positions.label: 0–10 years
positions.text: Ten years of The Hanged Man are a long halt between stations: the old route has stopped and the new one is visible only from another point. Outwardly there are few events, inwardly many: the pause pays off when the person comes out of it knowing what they will no longer do. The danger is not the standstill itself but the habit of treating waiting as the only strategy and writing off all ten years to it. Find the small action that stays available even with your hands tied, and do it.

positions.label: 10–20 years
positions.text: A Judgement period is going through a large archive: a postponed project, a professional choice and the family history all ask to be worked on again. In the version that works, the old project is picked up again with a correction for how it ended last time. What makes such a review empty is the readiness to call any return a sign of fate and repeat the plot without conclusions. Take one postponed project and name what will be done differently in it.

positions.label: 20–30 years
positions.text: A stretch under Justice lays contracts, calculations and conversations on the table that can no longer be kept in fog. What is sorted out fairly here serves for decades afterwards: terms made exact, deadlines named, your own share of the fault admitted. The most expensive habit is turning every story into a trial of yourself or of others. Rewrite one agreement to fit the conditions that have changed, instead of defending a rule that is no longer about this life.

positions.label: 30–40 years
positions.text: The decade of Strength is a climb with a heavy rucksack: a lot of work, responsibility for others, other people’s affairs that somehow became your own. People come out of such a climb tougher than they went in, if the weight was chosen to fit: what you took on can be carried for a year, and anything extra is handed back without guilt. Proving toughness at any cost is dangerous: the rucksack grows in silence, and those close to you notice first. Set the limit of one accepted responsibility in advance and check in a month whether it held.

positions.label: 40–50 years
positions.text: The World lays out an open map for these years: long trips, study, big projects, work that does not fit into one room. This is the right time to begin something that will take years — as long as the previous circle is closed and nothing is left owing on it. A new scale laid over unfinished obligations falls apart first, and instead of breadth you get scatter. Make two lists — finished and open — and close the open ones before taking on scale.

positions.label: 50–60 years
positions.text: The same arcanum as in “20–30 years”: the reading is above.

positions.label: 60–70 years
positions.text: A stretch of years under the Hierophant is a time to learn and to teach: a second education, mentoring, entering a profession for real. Decisions from these years hold when they were made for the sense of them and not for the gain: the person can explain their own work to someone else and is not embarrassed by the explanation. What breaks the stage is defending a familiar truth only because it has been yours for a long time: a student’s question gets a reference to your own experience instead of a look at their case. Test one of your beliefs by putting it to work: what it gives in practice now, not what it gave ten years ago.

positions.label: 70–80 years
positions.text: Under The Star these years are a desk buried in sketches of the future: creative work, study, meetings that set the direction for years ahead. Such a desk comes alive through plain daily work: one plan carried to a visible result pulls the rest after it. Ideas arrive faster than hands can reach them, and the decade goes on waiting for the perfect moment. Write down what you thought up — there are more ideas than memory holds — and finish at least one a year.

In the role of a decade this arcanum sets the theme of the stage and the question that gradually becomes the main one: A stretch of years under the Hierophant is a time to learn and to teach: a second education, mentoring, entering a profession for real.
agePeriods.strength: Decisions from these years hold when they were made for the sense of them and not for the gain: the person can explain their own work to someone else and is not embarrassed by the explanation
agePeriods.risk: What breaks the stage is defending a familiar truth only because it has been yours for a long time: a student’s question gets a reference to your own experience instead of a look at their case
agePeriods.action: Test one of your beliefs by putting it to work: what it gives in practice now, not what it gave ten years ago.

agePeriods.title: The Star
agePeriods.essence: The 70–80 frame helps to join the stages already passed into one story, to see the repeating ways of choosing and to leave a new answer open; it judges neither the quality nor the length of a life. In the role of a decade this arcanum sets the theme of the stage and the question that gradually becomes the main one: Under The Star these years are a desk buried in sketches of the future: creative work, study, meetings that set the direction for years ahead.
agePeriods.strength: Such a desk comes alive through plain daily work: one plan carried to a visible result pulls the rest after it
agePeriods.risk: Ideas arrive faster than hands can reach them, and the decade goes on waiting for the perfect moment
agePeriods.action: Write down what you thought up — there are more ideas than memory holds — and finish at least one a year.
